Napoleon Bonaparte. Born in 1769 on Corsica, this man would rise from obscurity to become the French Revolution's greatest military hero and ultimately its usurper. He consolidated revolutionary gains into a personal empire that reshaped Europe. As a military officer during the revolution's wars against European monarchies, he built a reputation for tactical brilliance and innovative strategy. In October 1795, he suppressed the royalist Insurrection of 13 Vendémiaire, earning the government's trust and establishing himself as the revolution's indispensable military hero. His Italian campaigns from 1796 to 1797 were dazzling. He defeated Austrian armies and expanded French control while building his personal legend across Europe. He then conducted the Egyptian campaign from 1798 to 1799, attempting to threaten British interests in India. Though ultimately unsuccessful militarily, it enhanced his mythic status. In November 1799, he engineered the Coup of 18 Brumaire, overthrowing the ineffective Directory government and installing himself as First Consul, the revolution's strongman.

As First Consul and later Emperor, Napoleon consolidated revolutionary gains like legal equality, the abolition of feudalism, and meritocratic administration, but he systematically eliminated revolutionary democracy and restored order through autocracy. In December 1804, he crowned himself Emperor of the French, a symbolic transformation from revolutionary general to Continental monarch that both scandalized and inspired Europe. He established the Napoleonic Code, a civil law system that enshrined legal equality and property rights and became the model for legal systems across Europe and Latin America. He declared himself Emperor of Italy, King of the Netherlands, and Protector of the Confederation of the Rhine, redrawing the political map through conquest and alliance.

But his military ambition ultimately overreached. He defeated Austria repeatedly but faced mounting coalitions of European powers determined to contain French expansion. Britain remained undefeated and bankrolled his enemies. In 1812, he invaded Russia with the Grande Armée, over 600,000 soldiers. He expected a quick victory, but instead faced catastrophic losses in the harsh winter and impossibly long supply lines. He abdicated in 1814 and was exiled to Elba, but he escaped and returned for the Hundred Days from March to June 1815, only to be defeated definitively at Waterloo. He was exiled to the remote island of Saint Helena, where he died in 1821. Napoleon remains history's supreme example of the revolutionary who becomes the tyrant he fought against, and yet his paradox is that he genuinely transformed the institutions and ideologies of Europe.
